brief.situation: 10:00 at the triage desk of a busy emergency department. Four people arrived in the last few minutes; every bed is full, but the charge nurse will open a hallway bed for anyone you call level 1 or 2.
handover: Ms. Chen, 34: twisted her right ankle stepping off a curb; walks with a limp, swelling over the outer ankle; HR 82, RR 16, BP 126/78, SpO2 99%, pain 5/10.
Mr. Ortiz, 67: 'indigestion' since breakfast that goes to his jaw, sweaty and gray; diabetes, smoker; HR 96, RR 20, BP 152/88, SpO2 96%.
Ms. Diaz, 22: asthma, wheezing for two days, inhaler not helping; speaking in short phrases; HR 118, RR 28, SpO2 91%.
Mr. Brooks, 52: upper abdominal pain and nausea since last night, 'some dark stools'; takes ibuprofen for his back; HR 94, RR 18, BP 128/80, SpO2 98%.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Triage each person with the ESI decision points, then keep watching the waiting room: people change while they wait.
Partway through you are asked to write your reasoning. The case ends at 11:10, then a debrief scores what you did.

source.note: FLAG: authored. Mr. Brooks's upper GI bleed: untreated, his heart rate passes 100 about 15 minutes in and he faints in the waiting room at about 55 minutes. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: authored. 80 kg x 70 mL/kg (the ATLS rule of thumb as relayed in the CCRN Adult bleeding case, 2026-11-10). Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: authored. He faints and goes into shock in the waiting room at a 30% volume deficit (class III in the classic table). Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

FLAG: authored. Mr. Ortiz's ischemia: left in the waiting room, he goes into ventricular fibrillation about 30 minutes in. A teaching consequence, not a prediction. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.
FLAG: authored. Ms. Diaz's SpO2 falls about 0.08% a minute untreated. Simplified teaching model written for exam practice; not a validated physiological model.

cues.question: Which level did you give each patient and why, and what will make you change one?

parts.label: Levels and reasons
parts.criteria: Ms. Chen ESI 4 (one resource); Mr. Ortiz ESI 2 (high-risk situation: possible ACS); Ms. Diaz ESI 2 (danger-zone heart rate, respiratory rate and SpO2 in asthma); Mr. Brooks ESI 3 at arrival (two or more resources, vital signs acceptable).
parts.modelAnswer: Chen: stable ankle injury needing one resource (an x-ray), ESI 4. Ortiz: jaw-radiating 'indigestion' with sweating, diabetes and smoking is possible ACS, a high-risk situation: ESI 2. Diaz: heart rate 118, respiratory rate 28 and SpO2 91% in an asthma attack are danger-zone vital signs: ESI 2. Brooks: stable vital signs, will need labs and imaging: ESI 3 for now.

parts.label: When to re-triage
parts.criteria: Rechecks the waiting room by policy; re-triages Mr. Brooks to level 2 when his heart rate passes 100 or he becomes lightheaded or vomits blood, because dark stools on ibuprofen suggest an upper GI bleed.
parts.modelAnswer: Mr. Brooks's dark stools on ibuprofen could be an upper GI bleed. I recheck him within 30 minutes; a heart rate over 100, a falling pressure, lightheadedness or coffee-ground vomit makes him high risk, so I re-triage him to level 2 and get him a bed at once.

collapse.headline: A collapse in the waiting room
collapse.body: Find who was under-triaged or not rechecked: a high-risk situation, danger-zone vital signs, or a change while waiting.

safeTarget.headline: Decision points used, and the change caught
safeTarget.body: High risk before resources, resources counted right, the waiting room rechecked, and the patient who changed re-triaged at once. That is the expert path.

safeLate.headline: Everyone safe, by a slower route
safeLate.body: Check each level against the decision points, how fast triage went, when the waiting room was rechecked and how long the re-triage took.

scoring.modelReasoning: Use the ESI decision points in order. Mr. Ortiz's jaw-radiating 'indigestion' with sweating, diabetes and smoking is possible ACS, a high-risk situation: ESI 2 whatever his resource count. Ms. Diaz's heart rate of 118, respiratory rate of 28 and SpO2 of 91% in an asthma attack are danger-zone vital signs: ESI 2. Ms. Chen's ankle needs one resource (an x-ray): ESI 4. Mr. Brooks is stable at arrival and needs two or more resources: ESI 3, but his dark stools on ibuprofen make him one to watch. Recheck the waiting room; when his heart rate passes 100 and he vomits coffee grounds, re-triage him to ESI 2 and get him a bed at once.

dpQ.ask: Mr. Ortiz's vital signs are nearly normal. Why is he still level 2?

choices.label: He is not; normal vital signs make him level 3
A high-risk situation (decision point B) is level 2 whatever the resource count

dpQ.explain: ESI asks about high risk before it counts resources. Jaw-radiating 'indigestion' with sweating in a 67-year-old diabetic smoker is a high-risk situation, so he is level 2 even with acceptable vital signs.
